label: Internet and apps
rationale: Getting online and what you do there: looking things up, connection and signal trouble, and putting apps on your phone.
mixUps: netto de shiraberu (look things up, de for the means) vs netto ga tsunagaru (the net connects, ga). Phone signal is denpa, not shingou, and apuri o ireru uses the same 'put in' ireru as dengen o ireru.

targets.use: Said about checking facts, words and places online, often as an offer or a report: netto de shirabete miru (I'll look it up online), netto de shirabeta kedo wakannakatta (I looked it up but couldn't work it out). The de stays even in casual speech.
targets.notes: o marks what you look up (netto de imi o shiraberu), and netto o shiraberu (search the net) is fine too. To find something like a shop or a flat, the verb is sagasu: netto de sagasu. guguru (google it) is the casual verb: gugutte mita.

example.ja: ちょっとネットで調べてみる。
example.english: Let me look it up online.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっとネットで調べてみます。
examplePolite.english: Let me look it up online.

targets.politeJa: ネットがつながります
targets.trap: Not hataraku or ugoku: 'the Wi-Fi isn't working' is netto ga tsunagaranai ('doesn't connect'); ugokanai is for a frozen app or device.
targets.use: Said mostly in the negative when Wi-Fi fails: netto tsunagaranai (the internet isn't working). The same verb covers a call going through: denwa tsunagaranai.
targets.notes: Transitive half: netto ni tsunagu (connect to the internet). Slow internet is netto ga omoi ('heavy'): kyou netto omoi ne. Asking about Wi-Fi: koko waifai tonderu? (tobu 'fly', casual).

example.romaji: nanka netto tsunagaranai n da kedo.
example.ja: なんかネットつながらないんだけど。
example.english: The internet's not working for some reason.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka netto ga tsunagaranai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: なんかネットがつながらないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: The internet's not working for some reason.

targets.trap: Not shingou: phone signal is denpa ('radio waves'); shingou is a traffic light.
targets.use: Said when calls break up or pages won't load, usually without ga: koko denpa warui ne (the signal's bad here). On a call it comes as an apology: gomen, denpa warukute kikoenai (sorry, bad signal, I can't hear you).
targets.notes: A weak signal is denpa ga yowai; no signal at all is usually denpa hairanai, also denpa nai or kengai (out of range).

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa denpa ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここは電波が悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: The signal's bad here, isn't it?

targets.english: install an app, get an app
targets.trap: Not apuri o morau: English 'get the app' pulls toward morau, which sounds like someone handed it to you. Putting it on your phone is ireru ('put in').
targets.use: Said when recommending or setting up apps: kono apuri irete (get this app), mada irete nai (I haven't got it yet). Casual speech drops o. daunroodo suru is just as everyday (shop staff and signs use it), and younger speakers also say otosu (apuri otoshita). insutooru suru sounds more technical.
targets.notes: Deleting an app is apuri o kesu; updating it is appudeeto suru.

example.romaji: kono apuri irete mite, benri da yo.
example.ja: このアプリ入れてみて、便利だよ。
example.english: Try getting this app, it's handy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono apuri, benri desu yo. yokattara irete mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: このアプリ、便利ですよ。よかったら入れてみてください。
examplePolite.english: This app is handy. Give it a try if you like.
